title: Time Columns
description: Add and take away times in columns of hours, minutes and seconds, carrying at sixty or more and breaking an hour into sixty minutes, even across two empty columns.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

writeup.why: Add and take away times written in hours, minutes and seconds, carrying at sixty and breaking an hour into sixty minutes.
writeup.look: A column frame headed hours, minutes and seconds, with a sixty gate between each pair of columns and a check control under the answer.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Time Columns' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns worked against the columns in the frame, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column's answer lands and the second fixed at the columns this sum uses, two or three. On the fourth phase the check is counted as one more step. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The line of times runs across the top of the working area, 1060 by 56 at 76,214, holding the times of the question as written, each part on a card of its own. The column frame stands under it at the left, 600 by 430 at 76,286: three columns, each 180 wide, headed hours, minutes and seconds from left to right, the headings in ink. The hours column is vermilion, the minutes column deep blue and the seconds column reddish purple, the minutes and seconds columns each drawn with two places, and there is a line for each time, a near-black rule, and the answer line under it. A part dragged to the frame settles only under its own heading; dropped under another, it slides back to the line of times with its unit lit. A carry circle sits at the top of the hours column and of the minutes column, empty until something is carried. Between each pair of columns stands a sixty gate, a near-black bar across the rule with the word sixty on it. When a column's total is sixty or more the gate lights, sixty cells lift out of the column as one of the next unit, which rolls up and drops into the carry circle on the left in wine, and what is left goes down in two places, so a total of exactly sixty leaves 00. Below sixty the gate stays shut and nothing moves through it. The cell panel stands at the right, 440 by 230 at 700,286, and shows any sixty being carried or broken as sixty cells in six rows of ten. The break control sits under it, 210 by 56 at 700,540. It strikes through the digit on top in the column on the left and writes it one less above it in wine, and pours sixty cells into the column on the right, whose top figure is rewritten sixty more above it in wine. When the minutes and the seconds on top are both empty, the double break opens one hour into sixty minutes and then one of those minutes into sixty seconds, so the top line reads one hour fewer, fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds. The check control sits beside the break, 210 by 56 at 930,540, and the check strip under both, 440 by 110 at 700,612, adds the answer back to the smaller time in columns, with gates of its own, and lays the sum beside the larger time. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve keys three across, the ten digits and two keys that clear and go back, and the answer slot is split into hours, minutes and seconds under the same headings as the frame, the minutes and seconds boxes each with both places drawn so that seven minutes is written 07. Where a sum uses no seconds, the seconds box stands empty and is not asked for. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The hour hand, every hour tile and hour cell, the hours column, and the hours of a time the stage splits into hours and minutes are vermilion. The minute hand, every minute tile and minute cell, the minutes column and the minutes of a split time are deep blue. The second hand, every second cell and the seconds column are reddish purple. The a.m. half of the day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue on every strip, timeline and track, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber, so the label changes where the colour does. Time counted between a start and an end, every hop and total on a track, and the days counted between two dates are green. An hour or a minute carried or broken, with the digits it strikes and rewrites, is wine. A calendar day, week or year picked out or ticked, a month on its bar and a day tile are olive. The days left over beyond whole weeks, and the twenty-ninth of February in a leap year, are yellow outlined in near-black. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every clock rim, minute mark, clock number, hub, rule, tick, post, bracket, guide line and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because an hour hand is told from a minute hand by its length, a column by its heading, a half of the day by its label, and a counted day from one left out by being filled rather than outlined, before any of them is told by a colour. A figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. A column of time on this stage carries at sixty and not at ten or a hundred: the gate opens at sixty or more and at nothing less, and a carried or broken unit is drawn as sixty cells. A digit on top that goes down by one is struck through once and never rubbed out, so every break can be read after the sum is done.
writeup.finish: The card shows the child's last frame with every carry circle and every struck and rewritten digit still drawn, and the check written underneath.

phases.win: every number sits under its heading, and the columns are added one at a time from the seconds
phases.does: drags each part of each time under its own heading, then adds the columns from the right
phases.goal: each unit of a time is written in its own column, and the columns are added from the right, smallest unit first
phases.says: Put each part under its own heading. Which column do you add first?
phases.check: Away from the screen: add four hours ten minutes and two hours thirty-five seconds. What goes in the minutes column for the second time?
phases.feels: each column holds one kind of time, so a part is placed by its name and not by where the line ends
phases.hands: Give each pair a log sheet with columns headed hours, minutes and seconds. Read out two times, one of them with no minutes, such as three hours and forty seconds, and have the pairs write each part under its heading before anyone adds. Ask what goes in the minutes column of the time with no minutes.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which heading does each part belong under? Second rung, the phase's: which column is added first? Third rung: the frame is cut to two times in hours and minutes only, and the child places and adds them before the seconds come back. The pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: whole numbers are lined up at the right, and a time with a part missing is shorter than the other.
wrong.move: lines up two hours fifteen minutes thirty seconds and one hour twenty seconds by their right-hand ends, so the one hour stands under the fifteen minutes, and gets two hours sixteen minutes fifty seconds.
wrong.screen: the one hour card springs back from the minutes column to the line of times with its word hour lit, then settles under the hours heading, and the minutes of that line fill with 00. The columns are added again from the seconds, and the answer line reads three hours fifteen minutes fifty seconds beside the child's answer in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: seven is one digit, and the first empty place is where a digit goes first.
wrong.move: writes five hours seven minutes forty-two seconds with the seven in the first place of the minutes column, so the minutes read seventy.
wrong.screen: the minutes column's two places are both drawn, and the seven in the first place is read aloud as seventy minutes, an hour and ten minutes, while the gate beside it lights. The seven then moves to the second place with a nought in front of it, 07, the gate goes dark, and the child's line stays drawn beside the new one.

phases.screen: two times written in a line, and the empty frame headed hours, minutes and seconds
phases.soWhat: Write each unit in its own column and add the smallest unit first.

phases.win: one hour sits in a circle over the hours column, the minutes left are written with two digits, and the hours total takes in the carry
phases.does: adds the minutes, sends sixty through the gate as one hour, writes what is left, and adds the hours with the carry
phases.goal: sixty or more minutes carry an hour, and sixty or more seconds carry a minute, with exactly sixty carrying too
phases.says: The minutes make sixty or more. What goes over to the hours, and what is left?
phases.check: Add two hours forty minutes and three hours twenty minutes. What is written in the minutes column, and what is carried?
phases.feels: the gate lets sixty through the moment the column reaches it, and not one minute later
phases.hands: Write two study times on the board whose minutes add to exactly sixty, such as one hour thirty-five minutes and two hours twenty-five minutes, and ask whether anything is carried. Let the class argue, then count sixty minutes into one hour together and write the answer with 00 minutes. Then try three times whose minutes add to one hundred and twenty.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what do the minutes add up to? Second rung, the phase's: is that sixty or more? Third rung: the frame is cut to two times whose minutes make a little over sixty, and the child carries before the larger sum comes back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: in whole numbers a column carries at ten, and two places look full only at a hundred.
wrong.move: writes eight hours eighty-five minutes for six hours forty-eight minutes and two hours thirty-seven minutes, carrying nothing because eighty-five is less than a hundred.
wrong.screen: the minutes column adds to eighty-five and the sixty gate lights: sixty cells lift out, roll up into one hour and drop into the carry circle over the hours, and twenty-five go down. The hours then add with the carry, six and two and one, and the answer line reads nine hours twenty-five minutes beside the child's answer in the slot.

wrong.why: the chapter's summary box converts minutes only once they go past sixty, and sixty exactly seems to fit in the column.
wrong.move: writes three hours sixty minutes for one hour thirty minutes and two hours thirty minutes, because sixty did not seem to be past sixty.
wrong.screen: the minutes column adds to exactly sixty and the gate lights all the same: all sixty cells lift out and roll up into one hour in the carry circle, and the minutes left, none, go down as 00. The hours add with the carry to four, and the child's three hours sixty minutes stays in the slot beside four hours.

wrong.why: each carry met so far was a single one, so one feels like what a carry is.
wrong.move: carries only one hour when three sets of minutes add to one hundred and twenty, and writes four hours sixty minutes.
wrong.screen: the gate lights and one lot of sixty cells rolls into the carry circle, and the sixty left in the column are still sixty or more, so the gate lights again and a second hour rolls in beside the first. The minutes left, none, go down as 00, the carry circle reads two, and the hours add to five beside the child's answer.

phases.screen: a sum in the frame whose minutes add up to sixty or more, with the sixty gate waiting
phases.soWhat: Sixty or more minutes carry an hour, and what is left stays in the minutes column.

phases.win: the hours digit goes down by one, sixty minutes join the top minutes, and the difference is written
phases.does: breaks one hour into sixty minutes, adds them to the top minutes, and takes away column by column
phases.goal: when the minutes on top are too few, one hour is broken into sixty minutes and the hours go down by one
phases.says: There are not enough minutes on top. What can one hour give you?
phases.check: Take one hour fifty-five minutes away from four hours thirty minutes. Say what the thirty became.
phases.feels: the broken hour does not vanish, it crosses into the minutes as sixty
phases.hands: Write five hours ten minutes take away two hours forty minutes on the board, and ask whether forty can come from ten. Swap one hour for sixty minutes using a strip of sixty squares in six rows of ten, and write the hours one less and the minutes seventy. Then take away column by column.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are there enough minutes on top? Second rung, the phase's: how many minutes does one hour give? Third rung: the frame is cut to one hour and a few minutes on top with more minutes below, and the child breaks the hour before the larger take-away comes back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: the minutes column holds two numbers, and taking the smaller from the larger is the only take-away that seems to work, whichever line each is on.
wrong.move: takes the smaller number from the larger in the minutes column, fifty less twenty-five, and writes five hours twenty-five minutes for eight hours twenty-five minutes take away three hours fifty minutes.
wrong.screen: the minutes cell stays shut on the twenty-five on top, and the child's twenty-five is written small beside it. The break control strikes through the eight and writes seven above it in wine, and sixty cells in six rows of ten pour into the minutes on top, which are rewritten eighty-five. Eighty-five less fifty is taken away, and the answer line reads four hours thirty-five minutes beside the child's answer in the slot.

wrong.why: breaking a ten or a hundred is the regrouping practised with whole numbers, and a hundred seems to be what one of anything breaks into.
wrong.move: breaks an hour into a hundred minutes, writes the top minutes as one hundred and twenty-five, and gets four hours seventy-five minutes.
wrong.screen: the cell panel lays out the broken hour as it really opens, six rows of ten, sixty cells, and the child's hundred is laid beside it as ten rows of ten, four rows too many. The top minutes are rewritten twenty-five and sixty, eighty-five, and the take-away runs again, the child's answer staying in the slot.

wrong.why: the sixty minutes are the part that gets written, and the hour they came from is easy to forget to take off.
wrong.move: breaks the hour into sixty minutes but leaves the eight hours on top as they were, and gets five hours thirty-five minutes.
wrong.screen: the eight on top is lit with nothing struck through it, beside sixty minutes that came from nowhere, and the whole top line is counted in minutes to show it has grown by an hour. The eight is then struck through and seven written above it in wine, and the hours take away again, the child's answer staying in the slot.

phases.screen: a taking-away in the frame whose top minutes are fewer than the minutes below them
phases.soWhat: When the minutes on top are too few, break one hour into sixty minutes and take one off the hours.

phases.win: the top line reads one hour fewer, fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds, each column takes away, and the check rebuilds the top
phases.does: breaks one hour into sixty minutes, then one of those minutes into sixty seconds, and takes away column by column
phases.goal: when the minutes and seconds on top are both empty, one hour is broken into fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds
phases.says: The minutes and seconds on top are empty. How can one hour fill both?
phases.check: Take two hours ten minutes five seconds away from five hours. What does five hours become first?
phases.feels: one hour has to fill two empty columns, so one of its minutes is opened again into seconds
phases.hands: Write three hours take away one hour twenty minutes fifteen seconds, with 00 in the empty minutes and seconds on top. Ask where seconds can come from when there are none and no minutes either. Break one hour into sixty minutes on the board, then one of those minutes into sixty seconds, and write the top line as two hours fifty-nine minutes sixty seconds.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which columns on top are empty? Second rung, the phase's: what does one hour give when both columns need filling? Third rung: the frame is cut to one hour on top and a few seconds below, and the child breaks it twice before the larger take-away comes back. The pad stays open.

wrong.why: each empty column seems to need a sixty of its own, and breaking twice sounds like getting sixty twice.
wrong.move: writes six hours as five hours sixty minutes sixty seconds, which is one minute too many, and answers three hours twenty-four minutes fifteen seconds.
wrong.screen: the top line the child wrote is counted in seconds beside six hours, and it runs sixty seconds, one whole minute, past it. The double break then opens one hour into sixty minutes and one of those minutes into sixty seconds, so the minutes on top read fifty-nine, and the take-away runs again, the child's answer staying in the slot.

wrong.why: with nothing on top in two columns, the numbers below look as if there is nothing to take them from, so they come down as they are.
wrong.move: brings the thirty-six minutes and forty-five seconds straight down under the empty columns, and writes four hours thirty-six minutes forty-five seconds.
wrong.screen: the seconds cell stays shut over the empty seconds on top, and the child's numbers are written small beside the frame. The double break strikes through the six and writes five above it in wine, and the top line fills to fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds from the cell panel. Each column then takes away, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a whole number of hours on top, with hours, minutes and seconds to take away below it
phases.soWhat: Across two empty columns, one hour breaks into fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the check control runs on six hours take away two hours thirty-six minutes forty-five seconds. The answer, three hours twenty-three minutes fifteen seconds, slides down onto the smaller time, and the seconds make exactly sixty: the gate lights, a minute rolls into its circle, and 00 goes down. With the carry the minutes make exactly sixty too, that gate lights, an hour rolls into its circle, and 00 goes down again. The hours add to six, and the check strip reads six hours with both empty columns back, beside the top line it came from. It can be run as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase two times are written in a line across the top and the frame below is empty under its three headings. On the second a sum stands in the frame whose minutes will make sixty or more, with the gate between the minutes and the hours drawn shut and the carry circle empty. On the third a taking-away stands in the frame whose top minutes are fewer than the minutes under them, the minutes cell shut and the break control waiting. On the fourth a whole number of hours stands on the top line over empty minutes and seconds, with hours, minutes and seconds to take away below it. The running count at the top left holds the columns worked against the columns in the frame, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first part of the first time, or the minutes column, or the break control, or the empty minutes on top, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where each part goes. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two or three times in the frame, adding or taking away, with the sixty gates, the break control and the check control all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on writing times in columns, carrying at sixty or more, borrowing an hour or a minute, and borrowing across empty columns.
voiceLines: A frame with three columns, hours, minutes and seconds. Where does each part go?
Put each part under its own heading. Which column do you add first?
The minutes make sixty or more. What goes over to the hours, and what is left?
There are not enough minutes on top. What can one hour give you?
The minutes and seconds on top are empty. How can one hour fill both?
A new sum. Put each part under its heading before you add.
Free play. Any times in the frame, adding or taking away, with the gates, the break and the check open.
Work the column on the right first, and watch the gate at sixty.
Each part under its heading, each sixty carried, and each broken hour opened into sixty minutes.

observations.why: Each column holds one unit, so seconds are added only to seconds and minutes only to minutes.
observations.soWhat: Write each unit in its own column and add the smallest unit first.
observations.observe: Every part settled under its own heading, and the columns were added one at a time from the seconds.

observations.why: Sixty minutes make one hour, so each sixty in the minutes column belongs in the hours column.
observations.soWhat: Sixty or more minutes carry an hour, and what is left stays in the minutes column.
observations.observe: When the minutes came to sixty or more the gate lit, one hour rolled into the carry circle, and what was left went down in two places.

observations.why: One hour is sixty minutes, so breaking it moves sixty minutes across and leaves the hours one fewer.
observations.soWhat: When the minutes on top are too few, break one hour into sixty minutes and take one off the hours.
observations.observe: The hours digit on top went down by one, and sixty cells poured into the minutes on top.

observations.why: Sixty minutes are fifty-nine minutes and one more, and that one minute is sixty seconds.
observations.soWhat: Across two empty columns, one hour breaks into fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds.
observations.observe: With both columns on top empty, one hour opened into fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds, and the check rebuilt the whole hours.

phases.screen: two times written in a line, and the empty frame headed hours, minutes and seconds
phases.win: every number sits under its heading, and the columns are added one at a time from the seconds
phases.traceback: The parts settle under their own headings, the columns are added from the seconds, and the answer line reads the whole time.
ladder: Where do the seconds of both times stand?
Which heading do the 20 and the 16 stand under?
Minutes take two places. Which place does the 7 belong in?
Read the unit word after each number and find that heading.
Each column holds one unit, and the smallest unit is on the right.

phases.screen: a sum in the frame whose minutes add up to sixty or more, with the sixty gate waiting
phases.win: one hour sits in a circle over the hours column, the minutes left are written with two digits, and the hours total takes in the carry
phases.traceback: The minutes add up, the sixty gate lights, sixty cells roll into the carry circle as one hour, and what is left goes down in two places.
ladder: What do the minutes add up to?
Is exactly sixty minutes an hour as well?
After one hour goes over, are the minutes still sixty or more?
Is the minutes total sixty or more?
Take sixty out as one hour, then write the minutes that stay.

phases.screen: a taking-away in the frame whose top minutes are fewer than the minutes below them
phases.win: the hours digit goes down by one, sixty minutes join the top minutes, and the difference is written
phases.traceback: The break strikes the figure on the left of the short column and writes one less in wine, sixty cells pour into the short column, and each column takes away.
ladder: Can 25 minutes on top give 50?
Which minutes are on top, and which are below?
Here the seconds are short, not the minutes. Which column can give?
Break one from the column on the left of the short one.
The short column gets sixty more. Now take away each column.

phases.screen: a whole number of hours on top, with hours, minutes and seconds to take away below it
phases.win: the top line reads one hour fewer, fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds, each column takes away, and the check rebuilds the top
phases.traceback: The double break opens one hour into fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds, each column takes away, and the answer line reads the whole time.
ladder: Can the empty seconds on top give 45 seconds?
After the double break, how many minutes stay on top?
Can one hour give sixty minutes and sixty more seconds?

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The parts settle under their own headings, the columns are added from the seconds, and the answer line reads the whole time.
Phase 2: The minutes add up, the sixty gate lights, sixty cells roll into the carry circle as one hour, and what is left goes down in two places.
Phase 3: The break strikes the figure on the left of the short column and writes one less in wine, sixty cells pour into the short column, and each column takes away.
Phase 4: The double break opens one hour into fifty-nine minutes and sixty seconds, each column takes away, and the answer line reads the whole time.

voice.opening: A frame with three columns, hours, minutes and seconds. Where does each part go?
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Each part under its heading, each sixty carried, and each broken hour opened into sixty minutes.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted, speaking, voice, mascot, summaryRow, played, operation, rows, columnTotals, carries, breaks, checked, columnsWorked, columnsUsed, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files: correct, wrong (soft), win, and a tick when a piece snaps

voiceLines.en: A frame with three columns, hours, minutes and seconds. Where does each part go?
Put each part under its own heading. Which column do you add first?
The minutes make sixty or more. What goes over to the hours, and what is left?
There are not enough minutes on top. What can one hour give you?
The minutes and seconds on top are empty. How can one hour fill both?
A new sum. Put each part under its heading before you add.
Free play. Any times in the frame, adding or taking away, with the gates, the break and the check open.
Work the column on the right first, and watch the gate at sixty.
Each part under its heading, each sixty carried, and each broken hour opened into sixty minutes.
